clinicalPearls: Edwardsiella tarda is a Gram-negative bacillus of the Enterobacteriaceae found in freshwater and its fish, amphibian and reptile inhabitants
Human infection is usually acquired through contact with fish, reptiles or contaminated water, or ingestion of undercooked freshwater fish
Gastroenteritis is the commonest manifestation, ranging from mild watery diarrhoea to a dysenteric illness
Extraintestinal disease includes wound infection, abscesses, hepatobiliary infection and, uncommonly, bacteraemia
Serious systemic infection is more likely in hosts with liver disease, iron overload or immunosuppression
The organism produces hydrogen sulphide and is generally susceptible to agents such as fluoroquinolones, third-generation cephalosporins and aminoglycosides
Abscesses and necrotising soft-tissue infection require drainage or debridement alongside antibiotics
reference.pathophysiology: Edwardsiella tarda enters humans through the gastrointestinal tract after ingestion of contaminated water or freshwater fish, or through wounds exposed to aquatic environments and animals such as fish and reptiles. It can invade intestinal epithelial cells and survive within phagocytes, producing enterotoxins and haemolysins that contribute to diarrhoeal disease and to tissue invasion. In susceptible hosts, particularly those with hepatic disease or iron overload, it may disseminate to cause abscesses, hepatobiliary infection and bloodstream invasion, mirroring the pattern of other opportunistic enteric Gram-negative pathogens.
additionalDifferentials: Vibrio infections from marine or freshwater exposure
Other Enterobacteriaceae causing abscess or bacteraemia
additionalInvestigations: Culture of blood, abscess pus or wound tissue in invasive disease
Gram stain and biochemical identification, noting hydrogen sulphide production
Imaging to localise hepatobiliary or soft-tissue abscesses
Liver function and iron studies to identify predisposing conditions
Antimicrobial susceptibility testing to guide directed therapy
redFlags: Systemic sepsis in a patient with liver disease or iron overload after aquatic exposure
Deep abscess or hepatobiliary infection on imaging
Rapidly progressive wound infection following fish or reptile contact
reference.prognosis: Gastroenteritis is usually self-limiting, but invasive infection in compromised hosts, especially with hepatic disease, can be severe; timely antibiotics and drainage of collections generally lead to recovery.
pitfalls: Failing to ask about fish, reptile or freshwater exposure in a patient with diarrhoea or wound infection
Assuming all enteric Gram-negative isolates are commensal contaminants
Not draining abscesses when treating invasive disease
Underestimating risk in patients with liver disease or iron overload
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
management: Treat invasive infection with targeted antibiotics such as a fluoroquinolone, a third-generation cephalosporin or an aminoglycoside, guided by susceptibility testing
Manage gastroenteritis, which is usually self-limiting, with oral rehydration and fluid and electrolyte replacement, reserving antibiotics for severe or dysenteric disease
Drain hepatobiliary or soft-tissue abscesses and infected collections surgically or radiologically alongside antimicrobials
Resuscitate and provide organ support for bacteraemia and sepsis in compromised hosts
Identify and address predisposing conditions such as hepatic disease and iron overload with liver function and iron studies
Advise prevention through safe handling and thorough cooking of freshwater fish, wound care after aquatic exposure, and caution for immunocompromised and iron-overloaded patients
